g-a-posteriori.d: Known (or knowable) only through experience of the world. “Water boils at 100 °C at sea level.”

g-a-priori.d: Knowable independently of experience, beyond the experience needed to grasp the concepts involved. “7 + 5 = 12.”

g-abduction.d: Inference to a hypothesis because it would best explain the evidence; also called inference to the best explanation.

g-acceptance.d: Adopting a proposition as a premise for reasoning or action in some context, whether or not one believes it.

g-access-internalism.d: The view that whatever justifies a belief must be accessible to the believer by reflection.

g-ad-hoc-hypothesis.d: A modification introduced solely to save a theory from refutation, without independent testable consequences.

g-ad-hominem.d: Attacking the person who makes an argument rather than the argument itself.

g-affirming-the-consequent.d: The invalid form “If P then Q; Q; therefore P.”

g-agrippas-trilemma.d: The argument that every attempt at justification ends in an infinite regress, a circle, or an arbitrary assumption. Also called the Münchhausen trilemma.

g-ambiguity.d: Having two or more distinct meanings (lexical, syntactic, scope, collective/distributive). Distinct from vagueness.

g-analytic.d: True in virtue of meaning alone (or, for Kant, the predicate is contained in the subject concept). “All bachelors are unmarried.”

g-anchoring.d: The tendency for estimates to be pulled toward an initial value, even an irrelevant one.

g-anti-realism.d: The view that truth in some domain is tied to what we could verify or recognize, or (in philosophy of science) that we need not believe theories are true about unobservables.

g-apt-belief.d: Sosa’s term for a belief that is true because it manifests the believer’s competence.

g-argument.d: A set of statements in which some (premises) are offered as reasons for another (conclusion).

g-argument-from-ignorance.d: Concluding that something is true because it hasn’t been proven false, or vice versa.

g-argument-mapping.d: Diagramming the structure of reasoning: premises, conclusions, objections, and rebuttals.

g-availability-heuristic.d: Judging frequency or probability by how easily examples come to mind.

g-base-rate.d: The prior frequency of something in a population; ignoring it produces base rate neglect.

g-basic-belief.d: In foundationalism, a belief justified non-inferentially, not on the basis of other beliefs.

g-basing-relation.d: The relation between a belief and the reasons for which it is actually held.

g-bayes-theorem.d: The rule for updating the probability of a hypothesis given evidence: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio.

g-bayesian-epistemology.d: The theory that rational degrees of belief obey the probability axioms and are updated by conditionalization.

g-begging-the-question.d: Arguing in a way that assumes the conclusion; circular reasoning.

g-belief.d: The attitude of taking a proposition to be true.

g-brain-in-a-vat.d: A skeptical scenario in which a disembodied brain receives computer-generated experiences indistinguishable from normal life.

g-brier-score.d: A measure of the accuracy of probabilistic forecasts: the mean squared difference between forecast probabilities and outcomes.

g-bullshit-technical-sense.d: Speech produced with indifference to whether it is true (Frankfurt).

g-burden-of-proof.d: The obligation to support a claim; the party who bears it loses if no decisive argument is given.

g-calibration.d: The match between one’s confidence and one’s accuracy: being right about 70% of the time when 70% confident.

g-charity-principle-of.d: Interpreting others’ statements in the most reasonable way available.

g-closure-principle.d: If you know p and know that p entails q, you know (or are in a position to know) q.

g-cogency.d: The property of an inductive argument that is strong and has true (or acceptable) premises.

g-coherence-theory-of-truth.d: The view that a proposition is true if it coheres with a system of propositions.

g-coherentism.d: The view that beliefs are justified by their coherence with a whole system of beliefs, not by basic foundations.

g-conciliationism.d: The view that on learning that an epistemic peer disagrees, one should move substantially toward their view.

g-conditionalization.d: Updating credences by setting the new probability of H equal to the old conditional probability of H given the evidence learned.

g-confirmation-bias.d: The tendency to seek, interpret, and recall information in ways that confirm existing beliefs.

g-confounding.d: A third factor that causes both of two correlated variables, creating a misleading association.

g-conjunction-fallacy.d: Judging a conjunction (A and B) more probable than one of its parts.

g-consensus-scientific.d: Agreement among most experts in a field, usually resulting from convergent lines of evidence.

g-contextualism-epistemic.d: The view that the truth of “S knows that p” depends on the standards in play in the attributor’s context.

g-contingent.d: True but could have been false.

g-continuum-fallacy.d: Inferring that there is no real difference between X and Y because there is no sharp line between them.

g-correspondence-theory-of-truth.d: The view that a proposition is true if it corresponds to the facts.

g-credence.d: A degree of belief, represented as a number between 0 and 1.

g-critical-rationalism.d: Popper’s view that beliefs cannot be justified, only criticized, and that rationality consists in openness to criticism.

g-crux.d: A point on which a disagreement depends; settling it would change someone’s mind.

g-cynical-theory.d: Nagel’s name for the view that “knowledge” is merely a label for the opinions of the powerful.

g-de-re--de-dicto.d: The distinction between a claim about a thing (de re) and a claim about a proposition or description (de dicto).

g-deduction.d: Reasoning in which the premises are meant to guarantee the conclusion.

g-deep-disagreement.d: Disagreement over what counts as evidence or authority, so that the parties share no common ground for argument.

g-defeater.d: A consideration that removes or reduces a belief’s justification. Rebutting defeaters are reasons against the conclusion; undercutting defeaters are reasons against the support.

g-deflationism.d: The view that there is nothing substantial to say about the nature of truth beyond the T-schema.

g-demarcation-problem.d: The problem of distinguishing science from pseudoscience and non-science.

g-disjunctivism.d: The view that veridical perception and hallucination are fundamentally different kinds of mental state.

g-dogmatism-pryors-technical-sense.d: The view that perceptual experience gives immediate prima facie justification, without prior justification that perception is reliable.

g-doxastic.d: Pertaining to belief (from Greek doxa). The doxastic attitudes are belief, disbelief, and suspension of judgment.

g-doxastic-voluntarism.d: The view that we can choose what to believe.

g-dual-process-theory.d: The view that cognition involves fast, intuitive (System 1) and slow, deliberate (System 2) processes.

g-duhemquine-thesis.d: Hypotheses are tested only in conjunction with auxiliary assumptions, so a failed prediction does not show which hypothesis is false.

g-dunningkruger-effect.d: The finding that low performers overestimate their competence; its interpretation is disputed.

g-dutch-book.d: A set of bets that guarantees a loss; credences that violate probability axioms are vulnerable to one.

g-e--k.d: Williamson’s thesis that one’s evidence is exactly one’s knowledge.

g-echo-chamber.d: A social structure in which outside voices are actively discredited. Contrast with an epistemic bubble.

g-ecological-rationality.d: The view that heuristics are rational when adapted to the structure of the environment.

g-empiricism.d: The view that knowledge derives chiefly or entirely from experience.

g-epistemic-bubble.d: An information network from which other voices are omitted, but not discredited.

g-epistemic-egocentrism.d: The difficulty of setting aside one’s own knowledge when judging someone who knows less; also called the curse of knowledge.

g-epistemic-injustice.d: A wrong done to someone in their capacity as a knower, in testimonial or hermeneutical forms.

g-epistemic-luck.d: Luck in how a belief comes to be true. Veritic luck is incompatible with knowledge.

g-epistemic-vigilance.d: The largely unconscious monitoring of informants for competence and honesty.

g-epistemology.d: The study of knowledge, belief, evidence, justification, and rationality.

g-equivocation.d: Using a word in different senses within one argument.

g-essentially-contested-concept.d: A concept whose proper application is inherently disputed, such as democracy or justice (Gallie).

g-evidence.d: What makes a proposition more or less likely to be true; E is evidence for H if E is more probable given H than given not-H.

g-evidentialism.d: The view that a belief is justified if and only if it fits the believer’s evidence.

g-externalism.d: The view that justification or knowledge can depend on factors outside the subject’s awareness, such as reliability.

g-factive.d: A verb or state that entails the truth of its complement: “knows that p” entails p.

g-fallacy.d: A common pattern of bad reasoning that seems persuasive.

g-fallibilism.d: The view that we can know (or justifiably believe) something even though our grounds don’t guarantee its truth.

g-falsifiability.d: Popper’s criterion: a theory is scientific if some possible observation could refute it.

g-false-belief-task.d: A test of whether someone can attribute a mistaken belief to another; children typically pass explicit versions around age four or five.

g-family-resemblance.d: Wittgenstein’s term for a concept whose instances share overlapping similarities but no single common feature.

g-foundationalism.d: The view that justified beliefs rest ultimately on basic beliefs that are justified non-inferentially.

g-foundherentism.d: Haack’s hybrid of foundationalism and coherentism, modeled on a crossword puzzle.

g-framing-effect.d: Different choices produced by logically equivalent descriptions of the same options.

g-gettier-case.d: A case of justified true belief that is not knowledge because the belief is true by luck.

g-groupthink.d: A cohesive group’s tendency to suppress dissent and fail to consider alternatives.

g-grue.d: Goodman’s predicate (green if examined before t, blue otherwise) illustrating the new riddle of induction.

g-heuristic.d: A mental shortcut for judgment or decision.

g-higher-order-evidence.d: Evidence about one’s own capacity to evaluate evidence.

g-hinge-epistemology.d: The view, from Wittgenstein’s On Certainty, that some propositions are presupposed by all inquiry and are not themselves objects of doubt or evidence.

g-humes-fork.d: The division of all knowledge into relations of ideas and matters of fact.

g-illusion-of-explanatory-depth.d: Believing one understands how things work much better than one does.

g-illusory-truth-effect.d: Repeated statements are judged more likely to be true.

g-incommensurability.d: Kuhn’s claim that rival paradigms lack a common measure for comparison.

g-induction.d: Reasoning from observed cases to general conclusions or to unobserved cases.

g-inductive-risk.d: The risk of error in accepting or rejecting a hypothesis; its consequences affect how much evidence should be required.

g-infinitism.d: The view that justification comes from an infinite, non-repeating chain of available reasons.

g-information-cascade.d: A situation in which people follow others’ choices and ignore their own information, so that errors can lock in.

g-intellectual-humility.d: Being attentive to, and owning, one’s intellectual limitations.

g-intellectual-virtue.d: A character trait or ability that makes someone a good thinker, such as open-mindedness or intellectual courage.

g-interest-relative-invariantism.d: The view that “know” has a fixed meaning but whether a subject knows depends partly on what is at stake for that subject. Also called subject-sensitive invariantism.

g-internalism.d: The view that justification depends only on factors internal to the subject’s perspective.

g-isought-gap.d: Hume’s observation that no normative conclusion follows from purely factual premises.

g-justification.d: The property a belief has when it is held for good reasons or formed appropriately. Propositional justification is having good reasons available; doxastic justification is believing for good reasons.

g-justified-true-belief-jtb.d: The classical analysis of knowledge, refuted by Gettier.

g-kk-principle.d: If one knows p, one knows that one knows p.

g-knowledge-by-acquaintance.d: Direct familiarity with a thing, person, or experience (Russell).

g-knowledge-by-presence-ʿilm-ḥuḍūrī.d: Knowledge in which the object is immediately present to the knower without representation (Suhrawardī).

g-knowledge-first-epistemology.d: Williamson’s view that knowledge is basic and unanalyzable, and explains belief, evidence, and justification.

g-knowledge-how.d: Practical knowledge of how to do something.

g-likelihood-ratio.d: P(E | H) / P(E | not-H): how much more expected the evidence is if the hypothesis is true.

g-lockean-thesis.d: One should believe p if and only if one’s credence in p exceeds a threshold.

g-lottery-paradox.d: High credence that each ticket loses seems to justify believing each will lose, yet one ticket wins.

g-masked-man-fallacy.d: Substituting co-referring terms inside a belief or knowledge context.

g-meno-problem.d: Why is knowledge more valuable than true belief?

g-mindreading.d: The capacity to attribute mental states such as knowing, believing, and wanting to others; the source of our intuitions about who knows what.

g-modus-ponens.d: “If P then Q; P; therefore Q.” Modus tollens. “If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.”

g-mooreanism.d: Responding to skepticism by holding that we know ordinary truths (such as “I have hands”) better than any skeptical premise.

g-moral-encroachment.d: The view that moral considerations can affect what one is justified in believing.

g-motivated-reasoning.d: Reasoning driven by a desire to reach a particular conclusion.

g-motte-and-bailey.d: Advancing a bold claim and retreating to a modest one when challenged.

g-myside-bias.d: Evaluating and generating evidence in a way biased toward one’s own opinions.

g-myth-of-the-given.d: Sellars’s critique of the idea that experience provides non-conceptual foundations that can justify beliefs.

g-natural-frequencies.d: Presenting probabilities as counts of cases (“9 out of 98”), which improves reasoning.

g-naturalized-epistemology.d: Epistemology continuous with empirical science, especially psychology (Quine).

g-necessary-condition.d: Q is necessary for P if P cannot be true without Q.

g-necessary-truth.d: A truth that could not have been false.

g-neuraths-boat.d: The image of rebuilding a ship at sea: we must revise beliefs while relying on the rest.

g-no-miracles-argument.d: The success of science would be a miracle unless our theories were approximately true.

g-normative.d: Concerning what ought to be, rather than what is.

g-ockhams-razor.d: Don’t multiply entities beyond necessity; prefer simpler explanations, other things being equal.

g-open-mindedness.d: Willingness and ability to take alternative views seriously.

g-overconfidence.d: Overestimation, overplacement, or overprecision in one’s judgments.

g-p-value.d: The probability, assuming the null hypothesis and model, of data at least as extreme as those observed. Not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

g-paradigm.d: Kuhn’s term for the shared exemplars and framework of a scientific field.

g-peer-disagreement.d: Disagreement with someone who has the same evidence and is equally competent.

g-pessimistic-meta-induction.d: Many successful past theories were false, so current ones probably are too.

g-phenomenal-conservatism.d: If it seems to S that p, S thereby has some justification for p, absent defeaters.

g-pragmatic-encroachment.d: The view that practical stakes affect whether one knows or is justified.

g-pragmatism.d: The philosophical tradition of Peirce, James, and Dewey, linking meaning and truth to practice and inquiry.

g-pramāṇa.d: In Indian philosophy, a means of valid knowledge, such as perception, inference, or testimony.

g-preface-paradox.d: An author rationally believes each claim in her book, and also that at least one is false.

g-prior-probability.d: The probability of a hypothesis before considering new evidence.

g-problem-of-the-criterion.d: To identify knowledge we need criteria, and to test criteria we need known cases.

g-proposition.d: What a declarative sentence expresses; the bearer of truth and falsity.

g-propositional-knowledge.d: Knowing that something is the case.

g-prosecutors-fallacy.d: Confusing P(evidence | innocence) with P(innocence | evidence).

g-rationalism.d: The view that reason is a major source of knowledge, including substantive a priori knowledge.

g-reductio-ad-absurdum.d: Refuting a claim by showing it leads to a contradiction or absurdity.

g-reductionism-about-testimony.d: The view that testimonial justification reduces to perception, memory, and inference. Global reductionism appeals to the general track record of testimony; local reductionism requires specific reasons to trust each speaker.

g-reflective-equilibrium.d: Adjusting principles and case judgments against each other until they cohere.

g-regress-problem.d: If every justified belief requires justification from another, the chain must end, circle, or go on forever.

g-regression-to-the-mean.d: Extreme values tend to be followed by values closer to the average.

g-relativism.d: The view that truth, justification, or values are relative to a framework.

g-relevant-alternatives-theory.d: To know p, one must rule out relevant alternatives to p, not all alternatives.

g-reliabilism.d: The view that knowledge or justification depends on being produced by a reliable process.

g-replication-crisis.d: The discovery that many published findings fail to replicate.

g-representativeness-heuristic.d: Judging probability by resemblance to a typical case.

g-safety.d: A belief is safe if it could not easily have been false: in nearby worlds where one believes it, it is true.

g-scout-mindset.d: Galef’s term for the motivation to see things as they are, rather than defend one’s beliefs.

g-sensitivity.d: A belief is sensitive if, were it false, one would not hold it.

g-simpsons-paradox.d: A trend present in every subgroup can reverse when the groups are combined.

g-skepticism.d: The view that we know much less than we think, or nothing.

g-slippery-slope.d: Arguing that a first step will lead to a chain of consequences ending in disaster; sometimes fallacious, sometimes not.

g-social-constructionism.d: The view that some things taken as natural are products of social practices.

g-social-epistemology.d: The study of the social dimensions of knowledge.

g-sorites-paradox.d: The paradox of the heap, arising from vague predicates.

g-soundness.d: A deductive argument is sound if it is valid and its premises are true.

g-source-amnesia.d: Remembering a fact while forgetting where one learned it; a key test case for internalism.

g-standpoint-theory.d: The view that social position shapes knowledge and that marginalized positions can offer epistemic advantages.

g-stasis-theory.d: The classical method of locating a disagreement at fact, definition, quality, or procedure.

g-steelmanning.d: Constructing the strongest version of an opposing argument.

g-straw-man.d: Misrepresenting an opponent’s view as weaker, then refuting the misrepresentation.

g-sufficient-condition.d: P is sufficient for Q if P’s truth guarantees Q’s.

g-survivorship-bias.d: Drawing conclusions from the cases that survived a selection process, ignoring those that didn’t.

g-swamping-problem.d: If reliability matters only as a means to truth, it adds no value to a belief that is already true.

g-synthetic.d: True in virtue of how the world is, not meaning alone.

g-synthetic-a-priori.d: Kant’s category of truths that are substantive yet knowable independently of experience.

g-t-schema.d: “‘p’ is true if and only if p.”

g-testimonial-injustice.d: Giving a speaker less credibility than deserved because of identity prejudice.

g-testimony.d: Coming to believe something because someone told you.

g-theory-ladenness.d: The dependence of observation on the observer’s concepts and theories.

g-toulmin-model.d: A model of argument with claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, and rebuttal.

g-tracking.d: Nozick’s theory that knowledge requires sensitivity and adherence to the truth.

g-truth.d: On the most common view, correspondence with how things are; theories differ.

g-underdetermination.d: The situation in which the evidence is compatible with rival theories.

g-understanding.d: Grasping how things fit together and why, often thought more valuable than knowledge.

g-uniqueness-thesis.d: For any body of evidence, exactly one doxastic attitude is rational. Contrast with permissivism.

g-vagueness.d: Having borderline cases where it is unclear whether a term applies.

g-validity.d: A deductive argument is valid if it is impossible for its premises to be true and its conclusion false.

g-verbal-dispute.d: A disagreement that depends only on different uses of a word.

g-verification-principle.d: The logical positivists’ claim that a statement is meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable.

g-virtue-epistemology.d: Epistemology centered on the intellectual abilities and character of knowers.

g-warrant.d: Whatever turns true belief into knowledge (Plantinga’s term).

g-wisdom-of-crowds.d: The accuracy of aggregated independent judgments.

c-gettier.d: You can have a belief that is true, and justified, and still not know — because the justification and the truth were connected only by accident.

c-nofalse.d: The no-false-lemmas repair says a justified true belief is knowledge only if its justification does not depend on any false intermediate premise.

c-kinds.d: Knowing-that, knowing-how, and knowing-by-acquaintance are different epistemic achievements; a theory built for one should not silently govern the others.

c-value.d: The value problem asks why knowledge is better than merely getting the truth right by luck or by a method that happens to work once.

c-intext.d: Internalism says justification must be accessible from the subject’s perspective; externalism allows justification to depend on facts—such as reliability—that the subject need not know.

c-deont.d: Deontological justification treats epistemic justification as responsible belief-management: a belief is justified when holding it violates no epistemic duty.

c-basicality.d: A belief can be basic merely because you did not infer it from another belief, or basic in the stronger sense that its justification itself depends on no further justified proposition.

c-corr.d: A proposition is true when reality is as the proposition says it is: truth consists in a correspondence between truth-bearer and world.

c-cohtruth.d: On a coherence theory of truth, a proposition is true insofar as it belongs to the maximally coherent system of beliefs or propositions.

c-prag.d: Pragmatic theories connect truth to successful inquiry and practical consequences: what proves itself in disciplined experience, or what inquiry would converge on, is central to truth.

c-defl.d: Deflationism says “is true” does not name a deep property; saying “it is true that p” is, in the basic cases, just another way of asserting p.

c-object.d: Objectivity asks whether a claim’s truth or warranted status is independent of who judges it; relativism makes that status depend on a framework, standpoint, or standard.

c-percep.d: Perception is a primary source of empirical justification, but its epistemic puzzle is how an experience that can mislead nevertheless gives immediate reason to believe the world is as it appears.

c-dirreal.d: Direct realism says ordinary perception puts you in direct perceptual contact with mind-independent objects themselves, not with an inner intermediary that must be inferred beyond.

c-indreal.d: Indirect realism says we know external objects through perceptual representations: the external cause is real, but what is immediately available to consciousness is representational.

c-illus.d: The argument from illusion uses the similarity between deceptive and veridical experience to argue that what we immediately perceive cannot simply be the external object.

c-mem.d: Memory typically preserves justification and knowledge across time, but it can also distort, confabulate, and produce a mere seeming of remembering.

c-past.d: Skepticism about the past observes that present evidence underdetermines whether the remembered and recorded past actually occurred as we take it to have occurred.

c-intro.d: Introspection gives unusually direct access to some current mental states, but that access is privileged rather than infallible.

c-apriori.d: A priori justification is justification available independently of particular sensory experience, paradigmatically through reason, concepts, or understanding.

c-ratemp.d: Rationalism gives reason an independent route to substantive knowledge; empiricism insists that substantive knowledge ultimately earns its content from experience.

c-ansyn.d: Analytic claims are true by virtue of meanings or conceptual relations; synthetic claims depend on how the world is—and Quine challenged whether that boundary can be made principled.

c-reduct.d: Reductionism about testimony says testimonial justification must be earned from independent evidence of reliability; anti-reductionism says testimony carries default entitlement unless defeated.

c-reid.d: Reid’s default-trust view treats testimony as a basic social source of knowledge: humans are prima facie entitled to believe sincere testimony unless specific defeaters arise.

c-biv.d: The brain-in-a-vat scenario is a skeptical hypothesis designed to be evidentially indistinguishable from ordinary life, forcing the question of whether experience can rule out radical deception.

c-relalt.d: Relevant-alternatives theories say knowing p requires ruling out the error possibilities that are relevant in the context, not every logically possible alternative.

c-moore.d: An argument only succeeds if its premises are more credible than the denial of its conclusion — so when a valid argument reaches an absurd conclusion, you may reject a premise before identifying which one.

c-pyrrh.d: Pyrrhonian skepticism aims not to prove that knowledge is impossible, but to suspend judgment when opposing considerations remain equipollent.

c-cartes.d: Cartesian skepticism uses methodical doubt to strip away every belief vulnerable to deception until only what survives radical doubt can serve as a foundation.

c-cred.f: درجهٔ باور در برابر باورِ دوگانه
c-cred.d: Credences represent graded belief—how confident you are that a proposition is true—rather than forcing every epistemic state into belief or disbelief.

c-priors.d: The problem of priors asks what rationally constrains your starting probabilities before the current evidence is incorporated.

c-dutch.d: The Dutch book argument says probabilistic incoherence has a practical cost: inconsistent credences can be combined into bets that guarantee your loss.

c-calib.d: Calibration asks whether events you assign probability p to actually occur about p percent of the time across comparable predictions.

c-probint.d: Probability can mean long-run frequency, physical propensity, logical support, or rational degree of belief—and many disputes arise from switching interpretations midstream.

c-induct.d: No finite record of observed regularity logically entails that the same regularity will continue in unobserved cases.

c-grue.d: Goodman’s “grue” problem shows that evidence alone does not determine which predicates or patterns are projectible into the future.

c-raven.d: Hempel’s raven paradox shows that logical confirmation can assign positive evidential relevance to observations that intuitively seem almost irrelevant.

c-risky.d: A risky prediction is one a theory could easily have failed: it forbids a narrow set of outcomes rather than accommodating almost anything after the fact.

c-adhoc.d: An ad hoc rescue modifies a theory after trouble in a way that protects it from the anomaly without independently increasing testable content.

c-corrob.d: For Popper, corroboration is a record of surviving severe tests—not confirmation, probability, or inductive support for future success.

c-normal.d: Kuhn’s normal science is puzzle-solving within a shared paradigm: most researchers extend and refine the framework rather than continually testing its deepest commitments.

c-theoryladen.d: Theory-ladenness means observation is shaped by concepts, expectations, instruments, and background theory rather than arriving as completely neutral “raw facts.”

c-lakatos.d: Judge a research programme over time, not a theory at a moment: it is progressive if its adjustments predict new facts that turn out true, degenerating if they only absorb what already went wrong.

c-expl.d: Scientific explanation asks not merely whether a model predicts a phenomenon, but what relation—lawlike, causal, mechanistic, or unifying—makes the phenomenon intelligible.

c-realism.d: Scientific realism says successful mature theories are at least approximately true about both observables and unobservables; anti-realism resists that extra ontological commitment.

c-constemp.d: Constructive empiricism says science need only be empirically adequate: accepting a theory commits you to its observable success, not to literal belief in its unobservable ontology.

c-causal.d: Causal inference asks what would happen under intervention or in a counterfactual world, so causal conclusions require assumptions that observational association alone cannot supply.

c-ladder.d: Pearl’s ladder separates association, intervention, and counterfactuals: higher-rung questions require causal information that lower-rung observational patterns do not contain by themselves.

c-confound.d: A confounder is a common cause of treatment and outcome that can create or distort association; causal adjustment aims to block that backdoor path without opening new ones.

c-collider.d: A collider is a common effect of two variables; conditioning on it can create a spurious association between causes that were otherwise independent.

c-values.d: Because evidence rarely entails a hypothesis with certainty, deciding when evidence is “enough” depends partly on the consequences of error—and therefore on values.

c-pval.d: A p-value is a tail-area probability of data under a specified null model; it is not the probability the null is true, the effect is real, or the result will replicate.

c-forking.d: The garden of forking paths shows how many data-dependent but individually defensible analytic choices can inflate false positives even without conscious p-hacking.

c-pubbias.d: Publication bias makes the visible literature a selected sample: positive, novel, and statistically significant findings are more likely to enter the record than null or messy results.

c-expert.d: A non-expert should judge experts indirectly—by argument quality, peer agreement, independent credentials, incentives, and track record—rather than pretending to re-do the expert analysis.

c-aumann.d: Aumann’s agreement theorem shows that ideal Bayesian agents with common priors cannot “agree to disagree” once their posterior beliefs are common knowledge.

c-echo.f: اتاقِ پژواک در برابر حبابِ معرفتی
c-echo.d: A bubble merely leaves opposing voices out; an echo chamber actively discredits them — so exposure fixes the first and strengthens the second.

c-condorcet.d: Under independence and individual competence above chance, majority judgment becomes increasingly reliable as the group grows.

c-fem.d: Feminist epistemology studies how social position, power, and institutions shape who can know, what gets investigated, and which standards of credibility and objectivity are treated as neutral.

c-quine.d: Naturalized epistemology replaces or embeds the traditional quest for a priori justification with empirical study of how creatures actually transform sensory input into beliefs and theories.

c-hb.d: The heuristics-and-biases program studies predictable departures from normative benchmarks, but the benchmark, task design, and replication record are part of the epistemic evaluation too.

c-argth.d: The argumentative theory proposes that human reasoning is specialized for producing and evaluating arguments in social exchange, not primarily for solitary truth-maximization.

c-blind.d: The bias blind spot is the tendency to see cognitive biases more readily in other people than in oneself, even after learning about those biases.

c-ivice.d: Epistemic vices are stable habits or character traits—dogmatism, closed-mindedness, intellectual arrogance, negligence—that systematically obstruct knowledge and understanding.

c-scout.d: The scout mindset treats beliefs as maps to be corrected; the soldier mindset treats them as positions to be defended.

c-clifford.d: Clifford says insufficient evidence makes belief itself ethically wrong; James replies that some live, forced, momentous choices rationally permit commitment before evidence can decide.

c-bs.d: Bullshit is speech produced with indifference to whether it is true; unlike lying, its defining vice is lack of concern for truth rather than deliberate falsity.

c-moral.d: Moral epistemology asks whether normative judgments can be known, what could justify them, and whether moral disagreement is evidence against moral knowledge.

c-valid.d: Validity asks whether the conclusion must be true if the premises are true; soundness adds the separate requirement that the premises actually are true.

c-modus.d: Modus ponens transmits a condition forward; modus tollens uses a failed consequence to reject the condition. Both are valid, but only under a genuine conditional.

c-motte.d: A motte-and-bailey alternates between a bold useful claim and a modest defensible claim, borrowing the latter’s safety for the former’s impact.

c-authority.d: Appeal to authority is rational testimony when expertise is relevant and well-grounded; it becomes fallacious when status substitutes for reasons outside those conditions.

c-evidfid.d: Evidentialism about religious belief requires belief to answer to publicly or personally adequate evidence; fideism allows faith to have rational standing not reducible to ordinary evidential support.

c-reformed.d: Reformed epistemology argues that belief in God can be rational and warranted as properly basic rather than inferred from propositional evidence or argument.

c-properly.d: A properly basic belief is rationally held without inferential support because it arises in the right epistemic circumstances or cognitive basis.

c-flew.d: Flew’s falsification challenge asks what conceivable observation would count against a religious assertion; if every failure is absorbed by qualification, the claim risks losing empirical content.

c-fideism.d: Fideism holds that faith has an epistemic standing not dependent on ordinary evidential proof and may even begin where discursive reason reaches its limits.
